#5807. Alaska voters aren't ditching ranked choice voting, top-four primaries

A voter walks into a booth at the Valley Bible Chalet to cast his ballot on Election Day, Nov. 3, in Indian, Alaska. Lindsey Wasson/AP hide caption

A ballot measure that would have repealed Alaska's nonpartisan primary system and ranked choice voting has failed, according to an overnight race call by the Associated Press.

This is the second time Alaskans voted down an effort to repeal the state's unique election system, which voters first approved in 2020. A repeal effort in 2024 also failed narrowly.

This year, though, Alaska's system was under intense nationwide scrutiny, due to the inclusion of two candidates with the same name on the four-person U.S. Senate general election ballot. That race appears likely to move on to a ranked-choice tabulation.

"Alaskans of all political stripes have spoken: They want the freedom to vote for any candidate, regardless of party, in every taxpayer-funded election," Nick Troiano — the executive director of Unite America, a philanthropic venture fund that invests in nonpartisan electoral reform — said in a statement before the AP call. "At a time when most general elections across the country are essentially coronations, the Last Frontier is showing that a better way is possible. It is time to honor the voters' decision and move forward."

Just a few states have nonpartisan primary systems that allow voters of all political affiliations to vote on the same primary ballot. While California and Washington's systems allow the top two vote getters to advance to the general election, Alaska's system allows the top four candidates to move on. Then, if no candidate gets a majority of the general election vote, ranked choice voting is used to determine the winner.

Opponents of Alaska's elections say the current system is confusing and can be manipulated.

Those opponents seized on this year's closely watched Senate race, in which an independent candidate named Dan Sullivan was alleged to be a Democratic-backed spoiler recruited to siphon votes that were meant for the Republican incumbent, also named Dan Sullivan.

Democrats denied recruiting the independent Sullivan, who made the top-four general election ballot and has defended his candidacy.

However, proponents of Alaska's system have said that the state's ranked choice voting system could blunt the effects of any confusion. Voters had the ability to rank both Dan Sullivans and not rank Democrat Mary Peltola, for example.

Massachusetts voters this year decided not to switch to a top-two nonpartisan primary system. And during the last election cycle, in 2024, several states considered measures that would create a nonpartisan system similar to Alaska's. Voters rejected all of those ballot measures.

#5804. Solar and storage companies voice support for federal permitting reform

Hundreds of solar and storage companies have co-signed a letter addressed to Congress in support of the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA) (S. 5653).

“You can’t lower energy costs if you can’t build the energy projects, and these companies know that this bipartisan legislation will help get America building again,” said Tim Pawlenty, CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA), in a press release.

BAAJA was introduced in the Senate on Sept. 30 by Sen. Shelly Moore Capito (R-WV), and co-sponsored by Sen. Mike Lee (R-UT), Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-RI) and Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-NM). The legislation is focused on quickening permitting for a range of projects with federal oversight, many of them related to energy production. BAAJA specifically calls out solar photovoltaic systems, energy storage and on- and offshore wind, but also includes language for fossil fuel sources, such as natural gas, oil and coal.

If passed, the Senate bill would amend sections of the National Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act of 1973 with the goal of shortening project permitting windows. According to the text, it would change and reduce which projects would need to be reviewed under those acts, such as water quality certifications; shorten the length of review periods for projects; and would not require permits for oil and gas drilling on land not owned by the federal government.

BAAJA would also grant the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission the ability to issue permits for some electricity transmission projects.

According to a SEIA analysis, if BAAJA was passed, solar energy output could increase by 167 GW between 2028 and 2035. The companies that signed this letter to Congress believe that federal permitting practices are outdated, and permitting reform is a solution to lowering energy costs.

“The message from more than 300 companies comes as voters made clear in the midterm elections that lowering energy costs is a top concern,” the group stated in a press release. “Permitting reform is urgently needed to meet rising demand and get more reliable, affordable solar and storage projects built.”

BAAJA is currently under review by the Committee on Energy and Natural Resources.

#5793. 'We can't let them down' -- After midterm wins, Democrats turn to charting path ahead

Texas Senator-elect James Talarico speaks at the Mission Ballroom during the What's Next Denver political convention on Nov. 12, 2026. David Zalubowski/AP hide caption

DENVER — Democrats descended on Denver for a two-day conference that was half victory party, half sober look at the road ahead on delivering for the voters who elected them.

The "What's Next" conference, hosted by the group Majority Democrats, was scheduled long before Democrats outperformed expectations with their best electoral performance since Watergate. It brought together rising stars — like incoming Gov. Rob Sand in Iowa and Sen.-elect James Talarico in Texas — along with strategists, organizers, state and federal lawmakers and potential presidential contenders.

Held at a concert hall, with colorful artwork of party heavy hitters dotting the venue, Democrats attended sessions like "What Voters Want" and "What Needs To Change." The overwhelming emphasis from speakers was that Democrats have to earn back trust.

A compilation of posters on display at the What's Next conference in Denver on November 12, 2026. hide caption

"We won races in places where we haven't won in a long time, even in some places where we've never won. And the message shouldn't be that [voters] are fully embracing the Democratic Party," said Colorado Rep. Jason Crow in an interview.

"It took us decades to dig ourselves in a hole and to push people away from us, and it's going to take us more than one cycle to earn that trust," said Crow, who is one of the party's recruitment co-chairs.

Attendees cheer during the What's Next summit. Following the midterm elections, prominent Democrats and political insiders gathered for the event to evaluate election results, and debate party strategy. Mark Makela/Getty Images/Getty Images North America hide caption

Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party, took the party to task for not investing more in the South and in Black voters.

"When we say that Black voters are the base of our party, then I ask why are we not investing in a region of the country that on Tuesday night just proved everybody wrong of what is possible," said Clayton to much applause. "Rural America deserves the investment from the Democratic Party and we must run towards communities that our party has run away from."

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg said Democrats shouldn't rest on their laurels.

"I think we are adequately politically traumatized by the last few cycles, so that we will not draw the wrong lessons from all of this," Buttigieg said. "Because here's the thing: it is yet to be written whether what we just experienced is one more oscillation from one side to the other and back, or whether it is the beginning of a tectonic movement changing American politics."

He said Democrats can learn from the current White House on two fronts, by having: "a bias towards action and a readiness to get things done coming out of the gate and at the very same time a readiness to plan for the long-term," adding Democrats should come out of the gate strong, with a rapid-fire series of bills to lower the cost of living.

Presumptive next Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries told the audience he has plans to do just that, with a robust agenda that includes reversing Medicaid cuts, banning congressional stock trading and mid-decade redistricting, establishing a statutory right to abortion, and overturning the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision that did away with limits on political spending by corporations and unions.

The conference itself was peppered with potential presidential contenders, including Buttigieg, New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, and California Rep. Ro Khanna, one of the few progressive speakers.

No one announced an official run, but many gave previews of their theory of the case.

"I do think it's important that whoever we hire to be the chief executive of this country knows how to run something, knows how to get stuff done, knows how to not just have a vision but knows how to deliver on it," Shapiro told reporters.

Someone who was previously kicking the tires for a possible White House bid — Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen — told reporters he's no longer considering it, as he instead pursues the top leadership post in the Senate.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., speaks during the What's Next summit on Nov. 13 in Denver. Mark Makela/Getty Images/Getty Images North America hide caption

Throughout the conference, Democrats debated whether and how to work with the Trump administration in order to deliver meaningful change for voters.

"If slapping Trump's name on it and putting it in gold letters would get it through — hell yes, I would do that," said Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

"The American people cannot wait two years for change, so we must work with President Trump," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any American presidency."

But New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill added a note of caution, describing the president as a bad faith actor.

"The art of the deal to Trump is he figures out what you want, he leverages the you know what out of you, and keeps taking, taking, taking, and never delivers," Sherrill said. "My advice to Sen. Talarico is if Trump wants to work with us, we will lay out the agenda, and he can sign it."

#5789. Florida city cancels St. Patrick's Day parade, citing new anti-DEI law

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (shown here in October) signed the anti-DEI law that Delray Beach officials say prohibits them from putting on cultural celebrations, like a St. Patrick's Day parade. Alex Wong/Getty Images hide caption

One of the first casualties of a new Florida law that prohibits taxpayer dollars from going toward diversity initiatives is a St. Patrick's Day parade in a beach town that has been celebrating its Irish American community for nearly 60 years.

The city of Delray Beach announced this week that it was canceling its popular St. Patrick's Day festivities in compliance with a new law that takes effect on Jan. 1. The city will also withdraw its sponsorship of LGBTQ Pride celebrations in June, officials said.

The law, backed by Republican Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis is part of the state's ongoing crackdown on diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) initiatives that the governor has called discriminatory and said have "no place" in public institutions.

The city lawyer for Delray Beach, a community in southeast Florida with picturesque beaches and a historic downtown, told the mayor that any government-sponsored celebrations of culture, ethnicity or heritage that are not a national holiday (for example: Independence Day) could run afoul of the new anti-DEI law. So, Mayor Tom Carney said, he made the difficult decision to cancel one of the city's biggest events of the year.

In past years, the parade, an annual event since 1970, wound its way through the downtown core of Delray Beach with spectators lined up several-people deep along the route. Local businesses and organizations sponsored floats and giveaways. School bands played as they marched through the streets. Participants included members of the Ancient Order of Hibernians, the largest and oldest Irish Catholic organization in the country.

"I've said it's engrained in the DNA of Delray and I do mean that. It's one of our signature events," Carney, a Republican, told NPR.

The mayor said he's hopeful that the city can find a path forward — and a way to preserve the event.

If a private sponsor were to volunteer to take over the St. Patrick's Day parade, or the June Pride celebrations, Carney said, the city would gladly hand over the reins and support the continuation of these festivities.

"These types of events we should be celebrating because in this country, people can have these events. In other countries, you can't do this. We have great freedoms here," he said. "And if the community wants something and it's not against public policy then I would support them to do it if they're using private dollars. If we can do it, we should do it."

Carney, who is of Irish descent, said the parade was privately run until about eight years ago — so returning to a private-sponsorship model would be a callback to the parade's origins. His own family, he said, was involved in keeping the parade going during the 1980s and 1990s.

Delray Beach officials said they have been inundated with emails, calls and social media messages from constituents who are angry that the community's decades-long celebration had been axed.

"It was kind of a call to action to me," Carney said. "The community really wants to have it, so we should go ahead and have it, we just need to get it privately funded."

The governor, meanwhile, has accused Delray Beach of weaponizing the new anti-DEI measure to make a political point. DeSantis said the city was "engaging in "malicious compliance" in a message he posted on X following the city's cancellation announcement.

"What they are doing is not mandated by Florida law," the governor wrote. "It's just an attempt to make a political point — a point that legacy media will no doubt try to amplify. We've seen these stunts throughout the years. Rinse and repeat."

The mayor said the city is merely trying to stay out of trouble with the law. The measure, SB1134, asserts that any official that violates the provision could face civil or legal consequences.

"The legislation has unintended consequences. The governor may genuinely believe what he believes and I take him at his word; our city attorney came up with a different conclusion," Carney said. "I'm going to leave it at that."

#5788. A review of ‘Solar Roots: The Pioneers of PV’

By Tor “Solar Fred” Valenza | November 10, 2026

Was today’s modern solar industry inspired by off-grid California-living, marijuana-growing, Grateful Dead-loving hippies? That’s the main question explored in “Solar Roots: The Pioneers of PV,” a new documentary that recently premiered in Grass Valley, California.

The entertaining documentary traces the history, colorful characters, off-grid homeowners, solar educators and the entrepreneurs who embraced solar photovoltaic technology for vastly different reasons.

Shot on a shoestring budget with volunteers, “Solar Roots” may not have the polished production of a Hollywood documentary, but it is an untold story about the people and early solar and technology that led to the modern solar industry.

Since 2009, when I first started in the solar industry, I had heard jokes and anecdotes about the marijuana-growing hippies who sparked the residential solar industry. Until “Solar Roots,” no one had ever set up a camera to talk to those early solar pioneers and document why rural America became a hub of off-grid solar innovation.

Enter Jeff Spies, a longtime solar veteran and the documentary’s executive producer. In 2015, Spies organized a weekend party for the off-grid solar pioneers of Northern California, where he started his career in the mid-2000s. After hearing so many colorful stories about why these rural homesteaders bought $14/watt solar panels and started new solar installation and distribution businesses, Spies enlisted another solar industry veteran, Jason Vetterli, to travel to Southern California, Arizona, Oregon, Colorado and Wisconsin to capture these unique and personal stories on video.

This isn’t the first documentary about the solar industry or its challenges, and to be clear, Vetterli and Spies’ narrative is not about creating “the solar biz.” Truly, it’s about a particular tribe of solar early adopters. Through interviews, we learn about the 1970s, ’80s and ’90s counterculture movement and the people who stumbled into solar businesses out of necessity and good timing.

Listening to these stories, you quickly understand that none of these solar pioneers intended to get into the solar business to make millions or solve climate change. Their real motivations were tied to maintaining their independence from cities while having enough electricity to keep the lights on and the music playing while raising a family. Beyond the home applications, solar became a new water-pumping solution that supported the pioneers’ cash-only “agricultural” businesses.

Vetterli sets the film’s tone and theme with the first scene. Instead of fading in to a utility solar farm or suburban residential roofs, the film opens with a young hippie using a wire to connect a single 35-watt ARCO solar panel to a car battery that powers an old cassette boombox. He then inserts a Grateful Dead tape and presses play.

The Grateful Dead-inspired musical score, composed by Midnight North, a band whose members include another solar veteran, TJ Kanczuzewski, appropriately plays under the rest of the film’s narrative and interviews.

After a brief solar technology history lesson, Spies interviews the solar pioneers about the roots of their solar PV fascination, how they came to realize that solar could grow and impact their lives and their off-grid movement.

This realization wouldn’t have happened without the back-to-the-land movement. Buying land was inexpensive but getting a utility to build a power line to DIY houses in rural California cost millions. While living without electricity, we learn about their lives before and after PV.

Before PV, the pioneers had to jerry-rig their pickup trucks’ batteries to listen to music and use dangerous kerosene lanterns for light. Gasoline generators were loud, costly, required maintenance and were contrary to the quiet, remote lifestyle they wanted. After PV (and lead-acid batteries), the solar pioneers could enjoy light, music, small DC refrigerators for cold beer and fresh food, 12-volt TVs and other DC devices that were designed for camping.

After implementing solar PV into their own homesteads, the pioneers wanted to share their find with their neighbors. It was that desire to share the off-grid solar PV love that led to the early solar distributor businesses, publications and training centers — not a desire to make millions.

As businesses grew, cultures clashed. We hear the story of when corporate solar salespeople traveled to Humboldt County in three-piece suits to meet their best customers who are wearing T-shirts and jeans and carry the scent and cash of a “weedpreneur.”

While the majority of the film is about the people who wanted an off-grid lifestyle, Vetterli and Spies also interview the late 1990s PV code and policy pioneers. These solar people also wore suit, but they also saw grid-tied potential to make solar mainstream.

“Solar Roots” does a great job covering this off-grid to grid-tied transition, but the film only covers a fraction of the stories and people who inspired the multi-gigawatt and global solar industry that exists today, and that’s O.K. A single two-hour documentary could never cover all of the world’s solar pioneers, but we’re fortunate to have met these particular solar people. They may not have started the residential solar industry, but they certainly contributed to it.

Spies and Vetterli plan to release the entire documentary online in the coming months and have set up a mailing list at www.solar-roots.com for people to receive updates.

Tor “Solar Fred” Valenza is a former film and TV writer (Stargate SG-1, Dharma & Greg, The Dead Zone) and current chief solar public relations geek at UnThink Solar, a solar PR and communications firm.

Tor, Thank you for participating in the debut of Solar Roots – The Pioneers of PV. I was honored to have you at this historical event with many of the main characters of our story in attendance.

Tor, thank you for this review. As you know, I was at the Grass Valley premiere too, and the film is a delight. Its account of how solar cells, battery charging, and inverters developed is the best I have seen: clear, even-handed, and grounded in the people who made it happen, with phenomenal historical footage.

Having spent those years at ARCO Solar, I smiled at the opening scene with the 35-watt ARCO module, the car battery, and the Grateful Dead tape. The homesteaders in this film put those early modules to work, solved practical field problems, and showed what solar could make possible.

The path runs from the 12-volt appliances of those early days to today’s 800-volt DC data centers, and it is far from finished. I look forward to sharing the film with students when it is released online, so the next generation can see whose work they are building on.

Congratulations to Jeff Spies, Jason Vetterli, TJ Kanczuzewski, and everyone who helped preserve this history.

Charlie, It was wonderful seeing you at the debut of “Solar Roots – The Pioneers of PV”. I was deeply honored to hear you say our story was the most balanced accounting of the development of the PV industry. Thank you for supporting our project and for all your work in bringing this magical technology down from space and introducing it to regular folks all around the world.

#5785. Trump blasts judge for halting his Washington golf project and says he will appeal

Temporary fencing is seen at East Potomac Park, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption

WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a "highly destructive and political decision" from a federal judge after she ordered a two-week delay on renovations at a historic Washington public golf course that he has been trying to redevelop into a championship-level venue.

In a social media post, Trump said his administration will "immediately appeal, on an expedited basis" the temporary restraining order from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, which she issued just before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months.

"It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court," said Trump, who spent much of the weekend posting photos on his social media site of the golf course. "They don't call it Trash Island for no reason!"

Temporary fencing is seen at East Potomac Park, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. Tom Brenner/AP hide caption

Trump had announced work on the site along the Potomac River would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that the president's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something Trump has denied. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the judge's decision.

Reyes, in her ruling Saturday, noted that those posts presented a problem for the government, indicating that Trump's redevelopment plan was final and that the National Park Service "will close the Park to implement it."

Both points, she wrote, "favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

The order is in effect through Nov. 28. The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.

Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.

#5784. New Mexico wanted free childcare for all. This is what's worked — and what hasn't

Children wearing Halloween costumes play on the playground of Kids Campus in Santa Fe, N.M. Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR hide caption

Catch up on what you missed with our Education newsletter, sent weekly.

It's a hazy August morning, and Judyn Martinez is dropping her daughter off at Kids Campus, a sought-after childcare center in Santa Fe that is now free for any eligible family in New Mexico.

"It's an amazing school so far. She loves it. I love it," Martinez said. "Everyone's nice. She's learning, growing already."

A year ago this month, New Mexico became the first state to offer free childcare to every family, regardless of income. To qualify, families must be residents of New Mexico and adults in the house must be working, looking for work, in school or unable to work.

Many parents, including Martinez, told NPR that it's been life-changing.

"I'm really grateful for universal childcare because I wouldn't have been able to send her," Martinez said.

There's just one drawback for families: Right now, the state doesn't have the capacity to meet the demand, which has left some families waiting without childcare. Martinez said it took her about a year and half to get off the waitlist for Kids Campus — a waitlist that, today, has nearly 700 children on it.

When she first spoke with NPR in September, Lilia Doyle said her 2-year-old son was on six different waitlists.

"I'm 97th on a multi-hundred person waitlist. I'm 75th on something. And some, I'm not even getting calls back," Doyle said.

Doyle, a children's librarian with a background in early childhood education, lives in Santa Fe. She acknowledged that she's selective when it comes to childcare. Still, she said, it should be easier.

"I have great belief in this program, but as it currently stands, I think the rollout needs a lot, a lot of help."

Kids Campus is a sought-after childcare center, with a waitlist nearly 700 children long. Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR hide caption

According to the state, New Mexico has about 67,000 children 5 and under, and about 50% of them are enrolled in the universal childcare program. Some of the remaining families participate in other free public programs, like New Mexico PreK and Head Start.

But many children aren't enrolled in any public, free childcare program, and it's hard to know exactly how many are in Doyle's position, unable to access universal childcare because of limited capacity. New Mexico officials acknowledged to NPR that the program needs to expand.

In order to work for every family, the program will have to overcome both a shortage of childcare workers and childcare slots — two challenges that are also playing out at the national level.

Because of that, across the country, policymakers and childcare advocates are keeping a close eye on this Southwestern experiment.

Cynthia Osborne, who leads Vanderbilt University's Prenatal-to-3 Policy Impact Center, said New Mexico is "going to provide lessons that the rest of the states are going to have to pay attention to."

"If New Mexico can show us how to build the infrastructure, I think other states will say that's an investment that we should make."

But the challenges to building that infrastructure – and keeping costs under control – are very real.

The program has built-in safeguards in case economic downturns make it harder to pay for – and one of those safeguards was recently triggered: The annual Consumer Price Index rose above 3%, which means wealthier families – who make more than $198,000 for a household of four – will soon have to start making a copayment. According to the state's Early Childhood Education and Care Department, ECECD, that copay won't exceed $148.50 a month. The department says this change will affect about 10% of enrolled families, and will remain in effect through the fiscal year.

Like many states, New Mexico previously offered childcare subsidies to low-income families, and free childcare to the lowest-income families. For a while, the state was raising the income limits for those programs.

Kids Campus has capacity for about 130 children. "Nobody questions a wealthy family sending their kids to public school and it should be the same for early childhood," said Catron Allred, who oversees Kids Campus and the early childhood program at Santa Fe Community College. Nina Alexandria Riggio for NPR hide caption

Families, providers and grassroots organizers had also been campaigning to do away with those limits entirely. One of the big sticking points was how to pay for it, and the answer came in 2022, when New Mexicans voted to dedicate a portion of the state's Land Grant Permanent Fund to early childhood education. Much of that fund consists of taxes and royalties on the state's vast oil and gas production, and it's large enough to provide hundreds of millions of dollars to support childcare every year.

Then, in September 2025, Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham announced a plan for free, universal childcare and prekindergarten, which would begin Nov. 1 of that year. After it launched, the program was approved by the Democrat-majority state legislature and was officially written into law in March 2026.

Any licensed or registered childcare provider in New Mexico can participate in the program. The state offers higher reimbursements for centers that pay workers higher wages and operate a minimum of 10 hours, five days a week.

"I think childcare is a gamechanger for every single thing that a state ought to deliver for its families," Lujan Grisham told NPR.

The governor said this year is going "stunningly well."

"I can't go anywhere in New Mexico… where I don't have a parent tell me that this is life-changing and transformative," she said.

"We need to keep growing," Lujan Grisham said. "It is not a stagnant set of opportunities."

In 2025, ECECD set a goal to create 12,000 new childcare spots in the first few years of the program, but did not share a specific deadline with NPR. According to the department, they are more than halfway there.

It was no surprise that accessibility would be an issue for a program like this.

Nearly half of all U.S. children, ages 5 and under, live in a licensed childcare desert, where demand for care outpaces availability, according to the Center for American Progress, a left-leaning think tank.

Olga Grays, a childcare provider for more than 20 years, said she fields messages every day from desperate parents who she isn't able to give slots to. That's one reason she's part of a group chat that includes over 40 childcare providers in her area.

Olga Grays operates Mrs. Olga's Daycare out of her home in Las Cruces, N.M. Bree Lamb for NPR hide caption

"Every time somebody calls me, you know, I put their name and the age of their kids in that group. And I'm like, 'Does anybody have openings?' You know, but the sad thing is that not a lot of people have openings, especially for infants."

Grays, a single mother of five, operates out of her home in Las Cruces, in the southern part of the state.

At Mrs. Olga's Daycare, the living room has been transformed into a classroom, with cushioned, fall-safe floors. The outdoor space is part children's playground and part garden oasis.

"[The children] can play with water, with dirt, grass. They ground themselves. It makes a world of a difference," Grays said.

She wishes she didn't have to turn any children away.

At Mrs. Olga's Daycare, the living room has been transformed into a classroom, with cushioned, fall-safe floors. Bree Lamb for NPR hide caption

"I think that's one of our biggest issues right now, is making sure that we have enough spots available for everybody coming in," Grays said. "And I think that's one of the flaws that perhaps other states can learn from."

According to the Center for American Progress, rural areas especially struggle with childcare deserts — and New Mexico is very rural.

"It's not a lack of funding, it's a lack of providers," the state's speaker of the house, Javier Martinez, told NPR. He's a Democrat and an advocate for universal childcare. "We have communities that are miles from any type of population center. Hundreds of miles sometimes. And so there are communities where that market isn't quite there to support a business."

The program's current operating budget is almost $600 million.

But there's concern among some state lawmakers that it's projected to be about $50 million over budget this year.

"By calling it universal, all we've done is add the wealthier folks," said state Sen. Steve Lanier, a Republican representing the northwest corner of New Mexico.

Lanier sued to stop the governor's universal childcare initiative — a lawsuit that was ultimately unsuccessful.

He told NPR that the steep price tag for this program is why he only supports childcare assistance for some.

"My daughter's a school teacher. She has two young boys. She gets free childcare. So, from a personal view, I see where it is needed. I mean, that helps her and her family immensely," Lanier said. "But somebody that's making $450,000, $600,000, do they really need that assistance?"

Catron Allred, who oversees the early childhood center at Santa Fe Community College, doesn't see it that way.

"To me, I think it's a mentality of early childhood as a public good," she explained. "Nobody questions a wealthy family sending their kids to public school and it should be the same for early childhood."

While New Mexico is the only state with free, universal childcare right now, other states and cities have made progress in that direction, including Oregon, Connecticut, Washington, D.C., New York City and Vermont, which has tapped into payroll taxes for funding.

In New York City, which already has free prekindergarten for 3- and 4-year-olds, Mayor Zohran Mamdani recently rolled out free daycare for thousands of the city's 2-year-olds.

As in New Mexico, "Both the biggest challenge and opportunity in New York City is our scale," explained Emmy Liss, executive director of the Mayor's Office of Child Care and Early Childhood Education.

Children eat breakfast at Mrs. Olga's Daycare. Grays said she fields messages every day from desperate parents who she isn't able to give slots to. Bree Lamb for NPR hide caption

"We know that every family's childcare needs are different. We know that our diverse landscape of childcare providers offer a really wide mix of services that families value," Liss added. "But to build a system that incorporates all of those different providers and meets the needs of all of our families is a complex challenge."

Liss said the goal is to have free pre-k for every 2-year-old by the end of the mayor's first term. But instead of expanding access to everyone all at once, as New Mexico has done, she said the city is growing capacity "in parallel" with access by creating more slots and matching them with families.

"We are working to build the infrastructure, the workforce, the physical capacity and the support to providers to ensure that we can continue to scale access to care here," Liss told NPR.

She said her office has been in conversation with leaders in New Mexico, and has had the chance to learn from them. But ultimately, she said, "Our realities are different."

"I think we're making slightly different choices in how we are implementing expanded access to care, which is good. I think we should be making different choices, responsive to the needs we hear from New Yorkers."

Veronica Ramirez lives in Ohkay Owingeh, a federally recognized tribe and pueblo in northern New Mexico. She said she learned about universal childcare when it was in the news last year and decided to enroll her 2-year-old daughter.

"For my daughter, I think it's really opened doors for her," Ramirez told NPR.

"Just being able to be around other little human beings that are her age...I've seen her go up to other little kids in public and say hi or just start playing with them. And I'm like, 'Oh, well, she's social now. She's not clinging to mom only.' "

Olga Grays, a childcare provider for more than 20 years, reads to children at her daycare. Bree Lamb for NPR hide caption

For Ramirez, having consistent childcare has enabled her to do more nonprofit work, including as an outreach coordinator at a birth center that primarily serves indigenous clients in nearby Española. It helps that her 7-year-old son is in school for the same hours as her daughter is in daycare.

"Now I'm able to work more and make more money and support my family a little bit better," Ramirez said.

The childcare help has opened other doors for her, too.

"I'm trying to get my bachelor's. I had my son when I was 19, right when I graduated high school," Ramirez said. "It's taken me a little bit longer, but I'm getting closer to getting a degree."

A new paper from Arizona State University found that lower-income mothers in New Mexico have seen significant gains since free, universal childcare was enacted, with full-time employment increasing by 23%.

The outdoor space at Mrs. Olga's Daycare is part children's playground and part garden oasis. Bree Lamb for NPR hide caption

But for Lilia Doyle, in Santa Fe, working full-time won't be an option until she gets her son off a waitlist and into consistent childcare. When she first spoke to NPR in September, she said she and her family are living on her husband's income.

"Hopefully our finances will be able to absorb it," she said. "We'll buckle down, and we'll make it through, but … it's not ideal."

Then, in October, Doyle got some news: A childcare center told her they found a spot for her son – but it wouldn't open up until August 2027.

#5782. Senate advances federal energy permitting bill

The Senate is fast tracking legislation that would reduce permitting times for energy projects, but possibly to the detriment of longstanding policies protecting the environment.

The Associated Press reported that the Senate voted 73-25 to advance the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act of 2026 (BAAJA). The bill was drafted in response to growing electricity costs from sources like grid-connected hyperscale data centers. By reducing permitting times, energy projects, like solar energy or onshore oil drilling, could address rising energy costs.

However, environmental groups consider BAAJA a reckless response to an immediate need for more power. The bill would amend sections of the Natural Environmental Policy Act, Clean Water Act and Endangered Species Act of 1973 to shorten review periods for new projects, and reduce which projects actually require reviews under these acts.

“We shouldn’t and don’t need to endanger our wildlife just to save a few dollars on gas. We shouldn’t and don’t need to weaken the rules that protect our water from pollution in order to build more clean energy. We shouldn’t facilitate more global-warming air pollution. And we definitely shouldn’t be taking away the public’s right to weigh in on projects that can ruin their environment, make them sick and lessen their quality of life,” said Lisa Frank, executive director of Environment America.

Despite the bill’s threat to environmental measures, the Solar Energy Industries Association (SEIA) has voiced its support for BAAJA, as have hundreds of companies in the solar and energy storage industry. More than 300 groups co-signed a letter addressed to Congress yesterday imploring the House pass this bill.

“Americans urgently need lower energy costs, a better electric grid and more nergy made in the U.S.A. This bipartisan legislation delivers all three,” said Tim Pawlenty, CEO of SEIA.

SEIA conducted an analysis that claims passing BAAJA could spur 167 GW of new solar energy on the grid between 2028 and 2035, while curbing the country’s CO2 emissions by 20%.

“Updating and expediting transmission and clean energy permitting is essential to delivering lower costs, reduced air, water and climate pollution, protecting communities and expanding the grid for the American people,” said Loren Blackford, executive director of Sierra Club, in a press statement on Sunday. “But rushing legislation that erodes Tribal sovereignty and people’s right to have a say in what is built in their communities, abandons clean water safeguards and wildlife protections, while further enabling a rogue president that is waging a war on clean energy and our public lands is not an acceptable outcome.”

#5781. Midterm voters ended the long-running GOP dominance in state legislatures

Georgia state Rep. Carolyn Hugley, the party's nominee for speaker of the state House, speaks in front of members of the Democratic caucus Thursday in the capitol. Sarah Kallis/GPB News hide caption

The midterm elections saw historic changes in state legislatures.

Pennsylvania voters elected a Democratic majority in the state Senate for the first time since Jimmy Carter was president. Democrats in Texas will run the state House there for the first time in 24 years. The Georgia House will have a Democratic majority for the first time in more than 20 years.

The results reversed a GOP dominance in legislatures that began in 2010 and had solidified since.

Going into the midterms, Republicans controlled legislatures in 28 states and Democrats held 18. The remaining few were divided. Now, with some votes still being counted, it looks likely the Democrats will hold a 24-to-22 lead with others divided.

So far, Democrats have picked up seats in nearly every state that held legislative elections, according to data compiled by NPR. Democrats gained significant ground in unexpected, reliably Republican states, like Texas, Utah and Florida.

The shift could mean real change in people's lives as legislatures rewrite laws on taxes, reproductive rights, access to health care, school funding and other issues. Legislatures have also been important in promoting or blocking President Trump's agenda.

The Republican State Legislative Committee, which coordinates support for GOP candidates, blamed the losses on the national anti-incumbent mood and heavy spending for Democrats. "Ultimately, the results of this cycle underscore both the challenges Republicans face and the importance of maintaining a strong, sustained presence in the states," the group's president. Edith Jorge-Tuñón, wrote.

The president of their rival organization, Heather Williams of the Democratic Legislative Campaign Committee, said their wins "proved what is possible when you put statehouses at the center of a national strategy."

Some of the biggest changes could come in states where Democrats now control both chambers of the legislature and the governor's office. They gained six new "trifectas."

In Arizona, Democrats will have the majorities in the state House and Senate and hold the governor's office — a trifecta — for the first time since 1966.

One possible policy change could be on school vouchers. Gov. Katie Hobbs has repeatedly tried to reform and limit the state's billion-dollar voucher program, which provides public money for private school tuition regardless of family income. But the Republican-run legislature had blocked her. Arizona Democrats have said they also hope to provide financial relief on rent, utilities and childcare.

In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro has promised to work with a newly Democratic legislature to raise the minimum wage to $15 an hour, strengthen abortion rights and increase affordable housing.

Democrats also won trifectas in Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and in Nevada, where they won the governor's office. They broke Republican trifectas in Georgia, Iowa, New Hampshire, Ohio and Texas.

Going into the midterms, Republicans had a few more trifectas than the Democrats. Now Democrats will likely have 22 and the Republicans 17, with 10 other states divided, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. (That doesn't include Nebraska, with a Republican governor and a unicameral legislature controlled by Republicans.)

In some states, including Georgia, North Carolina and Texas, Democrats have turned Republican-controlled legislatures into divided legislatures.

Georgia Democrats won the House and came close in the Senate. On their agenda, they could try to win over a few GOP lawmakers and pass Medicaid expansion to provide health care to more low income residents. There could also be an effort by House Democrats to repeal that state's six-week abortion ban, but that could be a tough sell in the Senate.

Democrats won control the North Carolina state House. As for the state Senate, a Republican is leading the race for one seat by just over a couple hundred votes and it is likely headed to a recount. It will determine if Republicans have a one-seat majority or if the chamber will be tied. If it is tied, the Democratic lieutenant governor would be the tie-breaker.

North Carolina Democrats are expected to try and roll back some abortion restrictions. And Democratic Gov. Josh Stein has called on both parties to work on addressing affordability concerns once the legislature convenes.

In several states, Democrats fell short of flipping some Republican-held chambers but won enough seats to end Republican supermajorities. The Multistate government relations firm says that happened in six states that had GOP, veto-proof supermajorities.

That will matter most where there are Democratic governors, who now have leverage to veto GOP initiatives, like in North Carolina, Ohio and Kansas.

Colin Campbell of WUNC, Sarah Kallis of Georgia Public Broadcasting, Carmen Russell-Sluchansky of WHYY and Wayne Schutsky of KJZZ, contributed to this story.

#5777. Rubix Battery: Storage Designed for Solar Installers

By James Mast, Managing Partner, Rubix Battery

AI and data center growth, extreme weather, and baseload retirement are straining the US electric grid. For homeowners and businesses, reliable access to electricity is increasingly important. That need is driving solar battery adoption. Solar power with battery storage can help keep systems running when grid power is unavailable and give property owners greater control over energy.

Energy storage is becoming an increasingly important part of residential, commercial, and off-grid power systems. In fact, the off-grid power systems market is expected to increase to USD 7.35 billion by the year 2032, while growing at a Compounded Annual Growth Rate (CAGR) of 15.0%. For solar contractors, that growth brings new opportunities, but they will need battery solutions that accommodate different project requirements without adding needless complexity. As more customers consider storage, solar installers need battery solutions that can be configured for different loads, applications, and long-term goals.

Rubix Battery is a U.S.-based energy storage manufacturer specializing in lithium iron phosphate (LiFePO4) solar batteries. Drawing on personal, hands-on experience with solar and off-grid installations, the company develops battery systems with an emphasis on practical installation, scalable capacity, and long-term performance.

Battery specifications are important, but they’re only one part of what makes a battery good for a project. Installation requirements, wiring access, inverter compatibility, and the ability to expand a system all affect how well a product fits.

Rubix Battery knows what makes installation easier because the batteries were designed by installers with hands-on, real-world experience. They bring that knowledge and experience into product design. Features like enclosed wiring compartments, magnetic covers, modular stacking, and closed-loop communication with compatible inverters help simplify system setup. Integrated safety components and designs that eliminate the need for external racking or exposed cabling further streamline installation.

This installer-focused approach also gives contractors flexibility when planning systems for customers with different energy demands. No matter what type of project, both residential and off-grid, Rubix offers two battery platforms to address a range of storage needs while giving customers reliable energy storage that grows as their needs do.

Battery performance over time depends in part on how effectively individual cells remain balanced. Rubix Battery uses Impactiv Balancing™ technology in every battery to help maintain consistent voltage throughout the battery pack.

Unlike traditional passive balancing, which dissipates excess energy from higher-voltage cells as heat, Impactiv Balancing™ transfers energy from higher-voltage cells to lower-voltage cells. The system also incorporates dissipative balancing when a cell reaches a critically high voltage.

With Impactiv Balancing™, Rubix batteries balance cells at up to 20 times the speed of passive balancing and can add up to 30% more battery life. Effective cell balancing is an important consideration when evaluating battery capacity, performance, and long-term reliability for installers and system owners.

Rubix Battery offers two primary product lines: the modular Stack Series and the high-capacity R-Series. Both use LiFePO4 chemistry and include Impactiv Balancing™ technology, closed-loop communication with compatible inverters, and a 10-year warranty.

Rubix Stack Series solar batteries are modular LiFePO4 energy storage systems designed for residential and light commercial applications. Each Rubix Stack Series battery module delivers 5.12kWh of energy storage, scalable up to 32 batteries in parallel for a maximum system capacity of 163.84kWh.

Rubix R-Series solar batteries provide higher-capacity storage for demanding applications, including off-grid, agricultural, and larger energy systems. Each Rubix R-Series battery module delivers 14.336kWh to 16kWh of energy storage across three configurations (24V/560Ah, 48V/280Ah, and 48V/314Ah) and is scalable up to 63 batteries in parallel for a maximum system capacity of 1,008kWh.

Selecting a battery platform involves balancing capacity, installation requirements, and a customer’s long-term energy needs. Rubix Battery’s Stack Series and R-Series give installers two approaches to system design, from modular residential storage to high-capacity off-grid applications.

With LiFePO4 chemistry, Impactiv Balancing™ technology, and features designed around installation realities, Rubix Battery offers battery options for contractors working on a range of solar projects.

Explore the product specifications and connect with the team at Rubix Battery to learn more about its energy storage solutions.

#5772. Colorado nonprofit launches plug-in solar program ahead of new state law

By Marie DeFreitas, Contributor | November 10, 2026

A new Colorado nonprofit is looking to bring distributed solar to households that have traditionally been left out of the residential solar market.

Solar Access Colorado, which bills itself as the state’s first organization dedicated to plug-in and balcony solar systems, has launched with pre-orders for small-scale solar kits ahead of the implementation of Colorado House Bill 26-1007, also known as the Improve Customer Use of Distributed Resources bill. The legislation establishes consumer protections for qualifying portable-scale solar devices, including provisions intended to make adoption easier for renters and homeowners living in communities governed by homeowners associations.

The Denver-based organization is positioning plug-in solar as an alternative for residents who cannot install traditional rooftop systems because they rent, live in multifamily buildings or lack suitable roof space.

“Colorado has taken an important step toward expanding access to distributed solar energy,” said Adam Harris, founder of Solar Access Colorado. “We’re launching Solar Access Colorado to help renters, apartment residents and homeowners participate in the clean energy transition with practical, accessible solar solutions.”

HB26-1007 creates a framework for personal, portable-scale solar generation devices. Beginning Jan. 1, 2027, the law will protect qualifying systems from unreasonable restrictions on their installation, use and operation.

The legislation also addresses HOA restrictions by treating qualifying portable-scale solar devices as energy efficiency measures under Colorado’s common-interest-community laws. This could help expand access to solar for residents who previously faced restrictions on making property modifications.

However, the law does not eliminate all installation requirements. Reasonable safety-related restrictions remain permissible, including provisions addressing secure mounting, fire prevention, electrical overload and potential property damage.

Solar Access Colorado plans to help consumers understand the new regulatory landscape and navigate product requirements and installation considerations as the law takes effect. Its initial product offering is designed for balconies, patios, fences and other outdoor spaces, giving residents additional options for generating electricity without committing to a conventional rooftop installation.

Beyond product sales, Solar Access Colorado plans to work with municipalities, housing organizations, property managers and community groups to broaden access to plug-in solar. The nonprofit also intends to prioritize education and outreach to low-income communities and multifamily households.

As states explore policies supporting smaller, customer-sited generation systems, plug-in solar could become another entry point for residential clean energy adoption. Colorado’s upcoming legislation is providing a framework for that market to develop.

Helpful overview, especially the distinction between expanded access and remaining safety rules. One practical detail for Colorado readers: the enacted HB 26-1007 summary says portable-scale solar becomes an energy-efficiency measure on Jan. 1, 2027, while reasonable property restrictions and applicable fire/building-code requirements still remain. PluginForSolar.com tracks those effective dates and system/compatibility questions for readers comparing plug-in solar options.

#5767. FERC’s LaCerte weighs in on midterms, PJM and utility monopolies

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

“The only way we’re going to get out of the affordability mess is by building more things,” said David LaCerte, a commissioner at the agency.

Utility Dive met with David LaCerte, a member of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, on Monday at the National Association of Regulatory Utility Commissioners’ annual meeting in San Juan, Puerto Rico. Never shy about expressing his views, we wanted to hear his perspective on how federal energy regulators are dealing with large load interconnection, the PJM Interconnection and keeping electricity affordable.

LaCerte, a Republican, joined FERC in October 2025. In mid-May, the Senate voted to confirm him for a full term that ends in June 2031. Before joining FERC, he held key positions at the U.S. Office of Personnel Management and the U.S. Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board, and was Secretary of the Louisiana Department of Veterans Affairs.

This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

UTILITY DIVE: How could the midterm results affect FERC?

DAVID LACERTE: I think [the results are] helpful in many ways. Having Americans' voices be heard about these affordability issues, which have been top of mind for us for a long time, is helpful.

And I wish we'd have more [Congressional] oversight committee hearings. I wish we talked about these issues more because the more we can talk about it, the more we can educate our partners on the Hill as to what the real issues are and how we can actually solve them, not from a political sense, but the real-world economic sense. The more those conversations happen, the better. So I welcome more oversight.

From an outside view, it feels like the five FERC commissioners do a pretty good job of talking to each other and reaching consensus.

We can't let ideology get in the way of a lot of our decisions. Now, I think ideology does get in the way of a lot of [other] decisions, especially at the state level, when state politics get inserted — we just don't want a pipeline, or we just want to exclusively run offshore wind. I don't think those results are good for Americans. And if the market demands natural gas in a region, we need to find a way to get it to them.

Do you think if politics weren't involved, we probably wouldn't have offshore wind?

I think that's a legitimate question. Or would we have natural gas generators in Maryland? Right now, we can't have that conversation because politics are making decisions for us. If I had a magic wand, I would let every area of the country have an energy mix that makes economic sense for them.

I think you see a lot of compromise in this permit reform bill. There is hunger for bipartisanship and consensus for both parties to work together on these issues, and I think that's by and large what's on the table.

So the question becomes: We have Democrats coming in and controlling both the Senate and the House. Are we going to be parties that want to work together to actually build stuff, or do we want to just let the status quo be maintained?

The only way we're going to get out of the affordability mess is by building more things. The only way forward is by building more generation, building more transmission. And to do that, we need to clear the deck on roadblocks, which have stymied us for decades. That's what Americans want. That's what Americans deserve.

Are there things that you feel the power sector could be doing better?

There's some areas of the country that are doing better. You see generators being able to be incentivized more in some regions than others.

I think the [PJM Interconnection capacity] price collar has a lot to do with that as well. I think there's a lot of heartburn on the price collar that was implemented in the spring, and what we do with that price collar in the upcoming auction in May as well, because we have to send the right market signals. We can't expect investment to occur if no one's making money. So the right price signals are paramount. We can't live under this price collar forever. But we also need to protect consumers. We can't let the market run unfettered. Our mandate is to have just and reasonable rates and reliable electricity delivered. So we have to balance all these things. But it's an environment where, if we don't send the price signals, new gen will never come.

There's a whole range of issues PJM is dealing with — interconnection, governance, the backstop auction, the capacity auction — so, how are you feeling about how PJM's been responding?

I think PJM has shown more responsiveness as of late. But we still need faster action, and we have a stakeholder process there that has been proven to be detrimental to improvements in PJM. We have an entrenched incumbency in PJM that has, by and large, been successful in their own operations, but we need new entrants. We need new investment, and we need to focus on how governance impacts all of that. These states have opted into PJM, and a lot of their mandates now go through the region. So I do think it's important that the states have an appropriate-sized role in governance.

On cost allocation, formula rates and other issues, how do you think about transparency in terms of people understanding what's happening, what's in their rates?

Transparency has been a big problem in the entire utility industry, and a lot of that is just a product of how monopolies were created within the [Federal Power Act]. And for a while, we got by because the need to more strictly scrutinize the actual rates wasn't there ... because the cost crunch on the average American wasn't felt.

But now we're at a different period of time, and real Americans are struggling to pay their bills, and … we need to require more transparency in every angle, because I do think that the utilities have been incentivized to use some of their own knowledge of how electricity is distributed to their own advantage.

Do you see anything FERC can do around transparency?

I think you see that in some of our orders. We came out and we first required utilities to consider grid enhancing technologies and advanced transmission in their consideration of a new [transmission] line, and then we took that a step further. We said, not only do you have to consider it, you have to show why you didn't choose one of the other options. We need to let the market decide what is best for utilities and ratepayers, and to do that we need more transparency in the entire process.

We have all these new technologies that come on board, and we also have a heavily entrenched transmission lobby who are incentivized to build more stuff because they get that guaranteed rate of return. But if there is an instance where we can use a new technology that brings a resource online faster and cheaper, we need to show that we're being prudent because this is not our money. This is real Americans' money.

We’re at NARUC, so are there areas where states need to be stepping up?

I think we need to get the states more in line with large load retail tariffs. I want [the states] working in directions which dovetail their state-level retail tariffs on large loads to some of the work that we're doing at the federal level. And I think by pairing those two together, you're going to get an environment that protects consumers more. It provides more market certainty, and it gives all the investors the rules of the road.

I'm sure you're also hearing from states on things FERC should be doing better.

The No. 1 thing we'll hear about is just jurisdictional in nature because there has been an evolution — a necessary evolution — on where the line ends on retail services and where it begins on wholesale or interstate services, because as things are becoming more and more interconnected, that line gets blurred.

And also, over the past several decades, the federal courts have, in my opinion, expanded what FERC’s jurisdiction may be. I come from a state background. I’m a big advocate of states making decisions for their backyards. So it's paramount to me that we don't encroach upon that line unless we absolutely have to.

Do you see issues right now where FERC is dealing with the federal-state divide?

I think you can see where we went with the [Department of Energy’s large-load rulemaking request]. We declined a full rulemaking and instead incorporated a balance with each individual [regional transmission organization] coming back to us to show us that [its] large-load tariffs are not unjust and unreasonable. It also creates a dialog. It allows for comment for all those entities, and a region-specific comment, which I think is of paramount importance.

Otherwise, it’s a generic rulemaking, which in today's day and age, with electricity being so dynamic ... it just breeds staleness within some of your regulations. [In] the rulemaking process, the timeline, the comments, the reply comments, the protests and then the court challenges — because you have all your eggs in one basket with a rule.

#5765. California orders utilities to develop joint DER orchestration framework

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The October order also directed PG&E, SCE and SDG&E to “more explicitly” consider flexible demand, a move one regulator said could reduce interconnection delays.

The order aims to harness DERs to meet local electricity needs, support grid reliability, reduce or defer infrastructure upgrades, and advance California’s electrification and decarbonization goals, the CPUC said.

“Our decision moves the state toward a common framework for the utilities to manage and forecast DERs on our system, and create visibility for the California Independent System Operator,” CPUC Commissioner Darcie Houck said in a statement.

The order gives Pacific Gas & Electric, Southern California Edison and San Diego Gas & Electric one year to develop a joint DER orchestration proposal that meets dozens of CPUC requirements, including “open and interoperable” communication; data sharing; cybersecurity; ratepayer protections; clear customer participation pathways; recognizing locational and temporal value; and avoiding double compensation for DER owners.

The framework will be developed in a working group process that considers input from stakeholders representing ratepayers, energy service providers, community choice aggregators and others. The process will establish “a common set of rules and policies across California” that the utilities would implement over time based on technological readiness, the CPUC said.

The working group must consider a range of technical, market and customer-facing issues related to DER orchestration, including methodologies for assessing cost-effectiveness and cost-benefit balance; DERs’ visibility to distribution system operators; DER aggregators’ role; technology ownership; flexible dispatch; “fair and non-discriminatory participation” for both utility and non-utility DER providers; and performance measurement, monitoring and accountability, according to the CPUC’s order.

Separately, the CPUC ordered utilities to evaluate how flexible electric loads can mitigate grid constraints and advance electrification as DERs become more common on California’s grid. Like standardized DER orchestration, planning scenarios that contemplate load flexibility may also help reduce burdens on ratepayers, the commission said.

Planning scenarios that “more explicitly” account for flexible demand will complement existing demand planning scenarios and focus on how dynamic changes in electric load — from shifting electric vehicle charging times or charging and discharging stationary batteries — could affect the timing, size and need for grid upgrades, the CPUC said.

In a statement, CPUC Commissioner Christine Harada said the order would help California utilities make “better use of the grid we already have,” reduce interconnection delays and avoid costly system upgrades. It would also make it easier for homes and businesses to electrify, she said.

“Our decision gives families and businesses more options to charge a car, electrify a home, or expand operations while reducing the need for costly upgrades. Those options need to be easy to understand and easy to use, people shouldn’t need an engineering degree to benefit,” Harada said.

#5763. No home left behind: Scaling VPP participation while maintaining customer control

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

Utilities that redesign demand management programs around how customers actually behave will be the ones to boost participation and system flexibility, writes Uplight’s Gisela Glandt.

Gisela Glandt is vice president of virtual power plants at Uplight, a provider of utility demand management solutions.

Load growth is back, and it isn't slowing down. Electrification, data centers and extreme weather are pushing utilities to find flexible capacity faster than they can build it. Demand-side programs including demand response, virtual power plants, time-varying rates and energy efficiency are one of the few levers that scale quickly and cost-effectively — yet the industry keeps hitting the same wall.

Roughly 80% of customers say they want help managing their energy, but utilities are still seeing enrollment in demand management programs around 10% — despite larger incentives, more innovative technology, and more targeted marketing. What if the problem isn't the customers and instead is the process of asking them to raise their hand?

Opt-in utility program enrollment puts the burden on the customer: to understand the program, check to see if they are eligible, decide it's worth it, and then take action. The benefits and incentives can show up months down the road, and they may even forget about them. Most people don’t make it past enrollment and it’s not because of lack of interest. It simply involves too many steps and too much brain power.

The industry is shifting from programs customers must join to flexibility that's already embedded as a default or activated at the point of sale of a device, with no enrollment required. Where utilities have made this shift, customer participation climbs from 10% into the 70% to 100% range. One Midwestern utility that restructured a program from opt-in to opt-out scaled capacity four to five times faster — and had 70% to 80% of customers participate.

“Opt-out" can be translated as "no choice,” and that couldn’t be further from the truth. A well-designed built-in flexibility program ensures that the customer stays in control. Instead of asking everyone to opt in to participate, it lets anyone choose not to participate at any time, with control that's visible, immediate, and intuitively easy. However, default programs only work when customers are really in control.

Behavioral demand response programs cast the broadest net with no hardware required, no cost of entry, and are open to nearly every energy customer. That's what makes it the most equitable and accessible path in: it reaches the renters and non-device-owners that automated demand response leaves out.

Device manufacturer-based programs work the other angle, unlocking capacity that's already installed and sitting idle: smart thermostats, connected water heaters, electric vehicles and batteries not yet enrolled in anything. When enrollment happens by default at device setup — through OEM partnerships rather than a separate utility sign-up — that latent capacity becomes dispatchable. The shifts are smaller and steadier than a typical demand response event, but can have even greater impact as participation scales exponentially.

For both types of programs, customers have the option to participate and receive benefits, and there are no consequences if they opt out of a particular event or day.

Participation in demand-management programs is an affordability strategy. Every home added to a utility’s flexible base expands the pool of dispatchable megawatts — and the more flexibility utilities can call on, the more generation they can defer or avoid. Deferred capital is downward pressure on rates. With affordability under scrutiny from regulators and customers alike, participation stops being a program metric and becomes an affordability lever.

A low-friction entry program can be an on-ramp for higher value programs. Customers who join a behavioral or OEM-based demand response program are now more informed and better targets for automated demand response, time-varying rates, managed EV charging, energy efficiency and other programs.

The utilities that redesign enrollment around how customers actually behave, with effortless enrollment and complete customer control, will be the ones that close the participation gap. Reliability and affordability increasingly depend on getting this right, with energy customers seeing the most immediate benefits.

#5760. Constellation pursues hybrid capacity contracts alongside nuclear uprates

Let Utility Dive's free newsletter keep you informed, straight from your inbox.

The offering gives Constellation “a new way to pair the existing fleet with incremental capacity” by adding batteries, generation and demand response, CEO Joe Dominguez said.

Constellation Energy is pursuing a new kind of bilateral contract with large customers that combines clean baseload power generation — likely nuclear — with other capacity resources such as battery storage, demand response and new generation, executives said this week.

The company is calling the offering “Peak+” and bills it as a simpler, cheaper and more environmentally friendly alternative to new gas-fired generation for hyperscalers and other large power consumers.

“Peak+ is going to be broadly defined as bringing capacity solutions plus existing clean and reliable generation,” Joe Dominguez, Constellation’s chairman, president and CEO, said on a Monday quarterly earnings call with investors and stock analysts.

Constellation is introducing the hybrid contracts as construction delays, cost overruns, interconnection delays and long-term fuel-price uncertainty present material risks for power plant developers, he said. He also pointed to the “political tilt in this last election,” which he said raises the specter of stronger federal regulation on carbon emissions affecting fossil fuel-powered plants.

“Constellation Peak+ gives us a new way to pair the existing fleet with incremental capacity,” he said. “We could add batteries and generation supply at our plants given the vast amount of land that we own around the plants.”

A slide in Constellation’s third-quarter investor presentation showed Peak+ pricing $20/MWh to $50/MWh higher than the “floor” set by the federal production tax credit for nuclear power but lower than the $110/MWh to $130/MWh levelized cost of power from new-build combined-cycle gas turbines in the PJM Interconnection’s eastern region — where much of Constellation’s nuclear capacity sits — by 2032, assuming a $3,000/kW build cost.

The production tax credit pays nuclear generating units up to $15/MWh when revenues fall between $26/MWh and $44.75/MWh, Constellation says.

The company signed its first Peak+ customer for a 20-year agreement for 270 MW of “unit-contingent energy, capacity and attributes from our existing nuclear fleet,” according to a press release. Dominguez declined to identify the customer.

He said he still expects some customers will pursue new large power plants or off-grid solutions. However, pairing “simpler and less risky capacity solutions with our large volume of clean energy is a compelling solution,” he said.

At about 55 GW, the Baltimore-based independent power producer says it has the largest combined fleet of nuclear, natural gas and geothermal generation in the U.S.

About 22 GW of that is nuclear, much of it in the capacity-constrained PJM Interconnection.

The company has announced more than 1 GW of hyperscaler-backed capacity expansions at existing nuclear power plants in recent weeks, including an 890-MW agreement with Google and a 190-MW deal with Amazon.

“I know that there's been some chatter that once we sold the [nuclear power] uprates, our ability to contract the existing fleet would somehow be exhausted — it is not,” Dominguez said.

In addition to the new Peak+ contracts, the company has “not finished exploring uprates at plants,” he said.

Dominguez also said the company’s planned nuclear restart at the site formerly known as Three Mile Island — now renamed the Crane Clean Energy Center — is on track for the second half of 2027 with the first fuel assemblies and transformers are on site.

Separately, Constellation announced another addition to its non-nuclear generating fleet, which grew dramatically in the past year following its $16.4 billion combination with gas-heavy Calpine.

Constellation said in September that it would pay Shell Energy North America $715 million to buy the Rhode Island State Energy Center, a 609-MW combined-cycle gas-fired power plant in the ISO New England wholesale market. RISEC will run on a merchant basis, Constellation said.
